name: Carhartt-Yomi Dockworker's Quilted Flannel Jacket
description:
A no-nonsense quilted flannel jacket with a snap-button front and two deep cargo pockets at the hip. The shell is a heavy brushed cotton-poly blend in a faded buffalo plaid — red-black or navy-tan — and the interior is lined with dense polyester batting that traps heat without bulk. Collar flips up and stays. Cuffs are triple-stitched. The whole thing smells like machine oil after a week of real use, and nobody who wears one minds.

This jacket has been manufactured in some form since the 2040s, originally under the Carhartt heritage license before Yomi Industrial acquired the brand. The construction is overbuilt for the price point — the kind of garment that outlasts the job it was bought for. Shelf workers, dock crews, and warehouse hands wear it because it works. Tier 3 nostalgia buyers wear it because their grandparents did.
what_it_says: You work with your hands and you don't perform it. This jacket is a tool, not a statement — which, in Meridian 88, is a statement of its own.
worn_by: Shelf residents who scored a good find
story_hooks: The inside breast pocket has a hidden sewn-in sleeve — originally intended for work permits, now used to carry anything from forged IDs to folded debt notes.
A discontinued colorway from the 2180s has become a covert identifier for a Shelf mutual-aid collective — wearing the right plaid gets you a meal and a bunk, no questions asked.

A quality control defect in a 2197 production run left a batch of jackets with an extra layer of batting over the left side — not ballistic, but enough to slow a blade. Someone on the Shelf figured this out.
